prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical discovery of the quantum spin Hall effect and topological insulators, and its experimental observation in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: Reading the eight opening ballots, B047 is the candidate with the broadest support from members who do not share my subfield: Mehlig ranks it first, Danielsson and Lindroth second, Eriksson third, and I had it fourth. Kane and Mele identified a topological invariant rather than a broken symmetry as the organising principle for an insulator, and predicted protected edge transport as its measurable signature. Molenkamp's group then observed the edge channels in HgTe wells, so the prize would rest on a prediction that was tested and then generalised across many materials. The interpretation has been stable for fifteen years or more, which answers the maturity concern that I have to raise against several other candidates. I move B047 ahead of my own opening first choice for two reasons. Four colleagues independently flagged the proximity of circuit QED to the 2025 prize. And I am the member with the most to gain from, and the most reason to discount, an argument made from inside superconducting circuits.
statement.case_against: The attribution is the real weakness. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed the HgTe route that Molenkamp realised, Zhang cannot be recognised, and Hasan's three-dimensional ARPES work, together with Fu, Moore and others, is a distinct claim that a three-person cap excludes. The 2016 prize for topological phase transitions and phases of matter also covers adjacent conceptual ground, so the committee must decide that this is new ground and not a second helping. If we cannot settle the 2D versus 3D allocation fairly, B046 is the cleaner configuration even though fewer colleagues rank it.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks B047 first as a reclassification of insulators by a topological invariant, notes the omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang and of the 3D work, and asks how much new ground this adds beyond the 2016 prize.
responses.response: I agree with the originality argument and with the point that the field is overdue. On the 2016 overlap I would draw the line this way. The 2016 prize recognised topological defects and phase transitions in model systems, including the integer quantum Hall plateaus and the Haldane chain. B047 concerns a time-reversal-invariant, spin-orbit-driven topological insulator with a Z2 invariant that needs no magnetic field, and which was observed in real materials. I think that is a distinct discovery. Your remark about the missing HgTe theorists is the part I cannot dissolve, and I would rather state it openly in the citation wording than pretend the trio is complete.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B047 second, with Kane and Mele as the decisive theorists, and says the choice between Molenkamp and Hasan for the experimental slot is not settled by the supplied credit. She also ranks optical lattice clocks first.
responses.response: I agree that Molenkamp is the right experimental name for this configuration, because the 2D quantum spin Hall observation is the direct test of the Kane-Mele prediction and of the BHZ proposal, whereas Hasan's work belongs to the later 3D generalisation. I would not describe that choice as free of cost, though. On B010, I rank it eighth because I read it as a technological milestone building on territory partly recognised in 2005 and 2012. I do not dispute the 1e-18 accuracy or the redefinition of the second, and I accept that its two-person attribution is cleaner than B047's. If the committee weighs measurement achievements heavily it becomes a serious alternative, but I am not yet persuaded that it displaces a discovery in a new class of matter.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks first and trapped-ion theory second, and would credit circuit QED to the two experimentalists Schoelkopf and Wallraff, citing the possibility that the 2025 prize already covers the domain.
responses.response: I agree with your caution about 2025, and it is why I have moved circuit QED down from my opening first place. Declaring a conflict of subfield is not enough on its own, so I accept your point as a substantive argument and not a procedural one. I disagree on one thing. Dropping Blais from circuit QED is not obviously fairer, since the 2004 proposal was the theory step that made the architecture legible, so the split between theory and experiment would stay contested whichever pair we chose. On B046 I am with you: Cirac and Zoller are a clean pair and I count it my first alternative if B047's allocation cannot be settled.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks B051 first and B047 second, proposing Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan, with Mele left out, and calls the omission of Mele and of the HgTe theorists a real attribution problem.
responses.response: I disagree with leaving Mele out. The Z2 classification and the quantum spin Hall proposal in graphene came out of the Kane-Mele pair together, and the two papers are so closely linked that it is hard to credit one without the other. Adding Hasan in place of Mele would reward the 3D experiment while deleting half of the original theory. On B051 I see it as a strong candidate, ranked sixth by me only because the superconducting mechanism is unsettled and one of the key experimental contributors is a doctoral student. Your point that the experiment-plus-prediction pairing is clean is fair, and I would not oppose it if the committee prefers a younger field.

uncertainties: Whether Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang can be acknowledged in the citation wording without extending the credited names beyond three, and whether Molenkamp then carries the experimental credit alone.
Whether the 3D topological-insulator work (Hasan, Fu, Moore) is better treated as a second prize part in a later year.
How far the 2016 prize overlaps with topological insulators, which I believe the Z2 insulator distinguishes but have not checked against the committee's earlier discussions.
I have not verified the exact priority dates from the supplied files; my statements about the roles of each group come from my recollection of the literature.
statement.conflict_note: I direct the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology and work at Chalmers with Per Delsing and C. M. Wilson on superconducting circuits, and I am a frequent co-author with Anton Frisk Kockum. This is a direct connection to B041 (circuit QED) and more loosely to quantum-computing candidates such as B046 through WACQT, so I would recuse myself from any decision that places circuit QED in the prize and have lowered its weight in my configuration. No specific connection to B047 is apparent from the provided profile.
